theme: The nations rage, Peter’s Pentecost proclamation
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 2. The nations plot against the LORD and his Anointed, but the LORD installs his King. You met this psalm earlier in the plan; today read it through Acts 4, where the church prays it after the first arrests.
settingTheScene: Psalm 2 was a coronation psalm, sung when a king of David’s line took the throne. In the New Testament it is quoted as speaking of Jesus, the ultimate Anointed One. In Acts 4:25-26, the believers quote verses 1 and 2 as they pray after the arrest of Peter and John. They see Herod, Pilate, the nations, and the peoples of Israel as the fulfillment of the rage. Their confidence is that the one enthroned in heaven laughs.
observation: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” (v. 1).
“The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed” (v. 2).
“He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision” (v. 4).
“As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (v. 6).
“I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (v. 7).
“Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession” (v. 8).
“Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth” (v. 10).
“Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (v. 12).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a question that has echoed through history: “Why do the nations rage?” Power rises against God. The kings of the earth take counsel together against the LORD and his Anointed, saying, “Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us.” They want to be free of God’s rule.

The answer from heaven is surprising: “He who sits in the heavens laughs.” It is not a laugh of amusement but of contempt for the futility of the plan. The nations are not a threat to God. Then he speaks in his wrath: “As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill.” The decision is made. The King is installed.

Then the King himself speaks: “I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” In the Davidic covenant, the king was adopted as God’s son (2 Samuel 7:14). The New Testament sees the full meaning in Jesus. The Father said this at his baptism and the Transfiguration, and Paul says that Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection (Romans 1:4, Acts 13:33). The Son is promised the nations as his heritage and the ends of the earth as his possession. This is the Great Commission in the language of the Psalms. The nations belong to Christ, and the mission of Acts is the fulfillment. He will rule with an iron rod. The nations that do not submit will be broken.

The psalm ends with a call to the kings to be wise: “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son.” To kiss the Son is to pay homage, to submit. “Lest he be angry, and you perish in the way.” And the final line is a gospel invitation: “Blessed are all who take refuge in him.” The Son who will judge is also the refuge. The first psalm opened with “Blessed is the man,” and the second ends with “Blessed are all who take refuge in him.”

In Acts, the church faces the rage of the rulers. They pray this psalm, and the place is shaken. The King is on the throne, and their courage comes from knowing it.
connection: 2 Samuel 7:12-16 is the Davidic covenant behind the psalm. Psalm 89:26-27 repeats the sonship. Acts 4:25-28 and 13:33 quote Psalm 2. Hebrews 1:5 and 5:5 apply it to Christ. Matthew 3:17 and 17:5 echo verse 7. Revelation 2:26-27, 12:5, and 19:15 use the iron rod. Romans 1:4 says he was declared the Son of God by the resurrection. Philippians 2:9-11 describes the whole earth bowing.
application:
When the news makes you anxious about rulers and nations, read verse 4 and remember who sits in the heavens.

Submit an area of your life that you have kept back from Christ’s rule. Kiss the Son.

Take refuge in him today, by name, in prayer.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what rage and plotting you see around you.
Thank him for the King he has set on Zion.
